safetyNote: Avoid eating Chlorophyllum brunneum. The German mycological society lists it as a cause of gastrointestinal poisoning, and reactions vary between people. Its resemblance to other shaggy parasols makes self-identification unreliable. Contact a poison centre after suspected ingestion with symptoms.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: A stout parasol-like mushroom with a broad cap, initially rounded then convex to nearly flat. The cap surface breaks into large angular brown scales on a pale fibrous ground, while the central brown disc stays mostly smooth. The broad crowded gills are free and whitish, later dull cream or marked brownish where bruised. The plain pale stem bears a prominent, persistent, usually movable ring with a relatively simple single edge.

sections.title: Bulb and colour change
sections.text: The stem ends in a conspicuous, abrupt bulb with a sharp, sometimes upturned shoulder. Cutting or bruising the pale flesh produces orange or saffron tones that become reddish brown, especially in the stem. Preserve the whole base: a gradually swollen stem is more typical of some related taxa, including C. rhacodes.

sections.title: Habitat
sections.text: It is saprobic and favours rich, disturbed soils: gardens, compost heaps, wood-chip beds and planted areas. Fruiting varies by region and can occur from spring to autumn. Habitat supports identification but is not sufficient by itself.

sections.title: Similar species and evidence
sections.text: Chlorophyllum rhacodes is very similar, generally with a less abrupt bulb and a more complex double ring; microscopic examination can be needed. Macrolepiota procera has a characteristically patterned stem and different cap structure. The DGfM categorizes C. brunneum under gastrointestinal syndrome. Some North American guides discuss it as edible with variable digestive reactions, so the app follows the safer poison-list classification rather than implying universal tolerance.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate shows a whole specimen with its abrupt rimmed bulb, a longitudinal cut showing orange-red bruising, a cap viewed from above, and white free gills viewed from below. The ring is shown as a single structure.
